title: Identifying Structural Biases from Causal Mechanism Shifts
claim: Different hidden biases leave distinct signatures in which variables' mechanisms shift together across contexts, unlike independent shifts in the unbiased case.
layout: 3 panels side-by-side, graph above context-by-variable shift grid, highlighted cells
description: Three side-by-side rounded panels titled Unbiased, Hidden Confounding and Selection Bias. Each has a small causal graph G* at the top. The graph has nodes W, V, X and Y. Small hammer icons in different colors mark the context (c1 to c5) that intervenes on each node. In the confounding panel, V is circled with dotted edges. In the selection panel, V is a dotted box with dotted edges. Below each graph is a grid of conditional distributions (P_W, P_X|W, P_Y|W and so on) across contexts c1 to c5. Faded cells show unchanged mechanisms. Colored cells (purple, green, yellow, blue) show shifted mechanisms. In the unbiased panel, shifts fall in separate columns. In the biased panels, the purple shift in c1 spreads across several rows. The eye goes first to the colored cells.
caption: Structural biases introduce dependent mechanism shifts. We consider three systems of four variables across five different contexts. The unbiased system (left) exhibits independent mechanism shifts. Under confounding (center), an actual mechanism change on hidden confounder V in context c1, leads to observed mechanism changes in variables X|V, W and Y |V, W for the same context. Under selection on a hidden collider (right), a mechanism change on that collider (V ) leads to observed mechanism changes for all its ancestors, X, Y , and even W.
abstract: Causal discovery methods commonly assume that all data is independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) and that there are no unmeasured variables affecting the system. In practice, these assumptions are often violated, leading to inaccurate inference. In this paper, we study how to identify hidden confounding and selection biases from causal mechanism shifts. In particular, we show that structural biases lead to dependent mechanism shifts. That is, by considering for which variables the mechanisms change given data from different environments, we can tell which variables are unbiased, which are subject to hidden confounding, and which are undergoing selection bias. We formalize this into an empirically testable criterion based on mutual information, and show under which conditions it identifies structural biases. To tell which nodes are subject to what kind of bias, we introduce the StruBI algorithm. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that StruBI works well in practice, accurately recovering affected variable sets and types of biases, outperforming the state-of-the-art by a wide margin.
